description.value: This study examined whether adolescents with pediatric bipolar disorder have abnormal regional functional connectivity in distributed brain networks during an affective working memory task.

spans.text: This study examined whether adolescents with pediatric bipolar disorder (PBD) have abnormal regional functional connectivity in distributed brain networks during an affective working memory task.

value: We hypothesized that the data-driven ICA analyses would reveal functionally segregated networks related to face processing, working memory, and affect processing and regulation, encompassing regions found with previous conventional fMRI studies using similar paradigms.

We hypothesized that PBD patients relative to HC would show differences in regional functional connectivity in these brain networks, especially in regions involved in emotion processing, emotion evaluation, and emotion regulation.

we expected that in PBD dysfunctional connectivity in affective and regulatory regions may correlate with the severity of manic and depressive symptoms and/or with performance measures on the affective working memory task.

description.value: Observational cross-sectional comparison of adolescents with pediatric bipolar disorder and healthy controls.

value: PBD showed greater connectivity relative to HC in left DLPFC and caudate, and right VLPFC and medial PFC; PBD exhibited reduced connectivity relative to HC in the junction of right DLPFC/VLPFC, amygdala, bilateral STS, left mid OFC, precuneus, right perigenual ACC, and mid-cingulate gyrus.

Within this network, the PBD group exhibits increased engagement of fronto-striatal working memory regions relative to HC, possibly due to cognitive effort, coupled with reduced functional connectivity in regions involved in affect processing and in the integration of affect and working memory processes.

spans.text: As illustrated in Table 4 , t -tests in SPM5 (with AlphaSim corrected p <0.02) found that PBD showed greater connectivity relative to HC in left DLPFC and caudate, and right VLPFC and medial PFC (note that the right medial PFC exhibited reduced BOLD signal activation during the task in the overall network, as indicated by downward arrows in Table 4 ). PBD exhibited reduced connectivity relative to HC in the junction of right DLPFC/VLPFC, amygdala, bilateral STS and left mid OFC, and precuneus, as well as in right perigenual ACC and mid-cingulate gyrus (Note that the right perigenual ACC, right midcingulate gyrus, and the left OFC exhibited reduced BOLD signal activation during the task in the overall network map, as indicated by downward arrows in Table 4 ).
Therefore, this component was labeled the “Affect Evaluation and Regulation Network”

definition.value: PBD showed greater connectivity in this network in right dorsal ACC and bilateral medial PFC, and lesser connectivity in right VLPFC, amygdala, fusiform gyrus, putamen, posterior cingulate gyrus, bilateral insula, inferior parietal lobule, and STS

spans.text: In line with our hypotheses, two-sample t -tests carried out in SPM5 to examine group differences (with AlphaSim corrected p <0.02) revealed that during the task relative to HC, the PBD group showed greater connectivity in this network in right dorsal ACC and bilateral medial PFC, and lesser connectivity in right VLPFC, amygdala, fusiform gyrus, putamen, posterior cingulate gyrus, bilateral insula, inferior parietal lobule, and STS (See Table 5 and Fig. 4a, b ).

Finally, an important finding for this network resulted from an exploratory secondary analysis in which we further examined differential network engagement while processing angry and neutral faces within each group.
To our knowledge, this is the first whole-brain functional connectivity study conducted on functional networks underlying the interaction between affective and working memory systems in PBD.

The compromised ability to process and regulate emotions in PBD may be related to reduced functional connectivity, and presumed reduced neural communication, between these regions.

spans.text: The ability to regulate emotions relies on efficient communication between a distributed network of regions that are involved in bottom-up emotional perception and in top-down cognitive evaluation of emotions (Passarotti and Pavuluri, 2011 ).

specific_metric.value: ICA-derived regional functional connectivity within spatially distributed functional networks

spans.text: All participants' fMRI time series for the affective N-back task were analyzed using a group ICA algorithm (GIFT v1.3h; http://icatb.sourceforge.net ) (Calhoun et al., 2001 ).

source_definition.value: Between-subjects diagnostic group factor comparing pediatric bipolar disorder participants with healthy controls.

spans.text: This analysis showed which brain regions of any given component were specifically implicated in the “fit” of its time course to the canonical hemodynamic response model for angry or neutral blocks in each group separately.

model_settings.value: Group ICA used concatenated participant fMRI time series, two principal-component-analysis data-reduction stages, and a final Infomax ICA rotation producing 46 independent components. Components were back-reconstructed for individual participants; ICASSO was run 30 times using FastICA, with reliability >80% required. Spatial maps were tested with SPM5 voxel-wise one-sample and two-sample t-tests, using AlphaSim cluster correction (minimum cluster size 11 voxels, uncorrected p=0.01, corrected p<0.02).

estimator.value: Infomax independent component analysis with FastICA reliability assessment

spans.text: The data underwent a final ICA rotation using Infomax that produced 46 maximally independent components (Bell and Sejnowski, 1995 ).

software.value: GIFT v1.3h for group ICA; ICASSO/FastICA for component reliability; SPM5 for regression, ANOVA, spatial-map t-tests, and voxel-wise analyses; AlphaSim for cluster correction.
